results.title: Derived subgroups of p-groups as Frattini subgroups (Kourovka 16.11)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The conjecture of Ya. G. Berkovich that for every prime $p$ and every finite $p$-group $G$ there is a finite $p$-group $H$ whose Frattini subgroup $\Phi(H)$, the intersection of the maximal subgroups of $H$, is isomorphic to the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ of $G$.

results.title: Derived subgroups of p-groups need not be Frattini subgroups of p-groups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There exist a prime $p$ and a finite $p$-group $G$ such that for every finite $p$-group $H$, the Frattini subgroup $\Phi(H)$ of $H$ is not isomorphic to the derived subgroup $[G, G]$ of $G$. That is, the conjecture of Kourovka Problem 16.11 is false.

results.title: Perfectness of the intersection of the derived series (Kourovka 17.82)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The conjecture of R. Mikhailov that for every finitely presented group $G$, the intersection $D = \bigcap_{n} G^{(n)}$ of the terms $G^{(n)}$ of the derived series of $G$ satisfies $[D, D] = D$, that is, $D$ has trivial abelianization.

results.title: The intersection of the derived series need not be perfect
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There exists a finitely presented group $G$ such that the intersection $D = \bigcap_{n} G^{(n)}$ of the terms $G^{(n)}$ of the derived series of $G$ satisfies $[D, D] \ne D$. That is, the conjecture of Kourovka Problem 17.82 is false; the Kourovka Archive credits this answer to V. A. Roman'kov (2011).

results.title: Fermat quotient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, the Fermat quotient is the integer $q_p(a) = (a^{p-1} - 1)/p$, where $/$ is integer division rounding down. The division is exact, since $p$ divides $a^{p-1} - 1$ by Fermat's little theorem.

results.title: Formula for the Fermat quotient

results.title: Fermat quotient times the prime

results.title: The domain of the Volterra operator
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The space on which the Volterra operator acts is the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$, with the sup norm.

results.title: Clamping to the unit interval
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real number $t$, its clamp to the unit interval is $\max(0, \min(t, 1))$, regarded as a point of $[0, 1]$.

results.title: Extension by clamping
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, its extension to $\mathbb{R}$ is the function $t \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$.

results.title: The clamped extension is continuous
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, its extension $t \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

results.title: The clamped extension agrees with the original function on the unit interval
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every real $t$ with $0 \le t \le 1$, the extension $s \mapsto f(\max(0, \min(s, 1)))$ of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ takes the value $f(t)$ at $t$.

results.title: The clamped extension is bounded by the sup norm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every real $t$, the extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping satisfies $|f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))| \le \|f\|_\infty$, where $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in [0, 1]} |f(x)|$ is the sup norm of $f$.

results.title: Continuity of the Volterra primitive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, the function $x \mapsto \int_0^x \tilde f(t)\,dt$ on $[0, 1]$ is continuous, where $\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ is the extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping the argument into $[0, 1]$.

results.title: Sup-norm bound for the Volterra primitive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$, $\left|\int_0^x \tilde f(t)\,dt\right| \le \|f\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the sup norm of $f$ and $\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ is the extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping the argument into $[0, 1]$.

results.title: The Volterra operator as a linear map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The real-linear map $V$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ given by $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ for $x \in [0, 1]$.

results.title: Sup-norm bound for the Volterra linear map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, the Volterra linear map $V$ satisfies $\|Vf\| \le 1 \cdot \|f\|$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the sup norm.

results.title: The Volterra operator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The bounded real-linear operator $V$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ (equivalently $C([0, 1], \mathbb{R})$ with the sup norm) given by $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ for $x \in [0, 1]$.

results.title: Evaluation formula for the Volterra operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$, the Volterra operator $V$ satisfies $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x \tilde f(t)\,dt$, where $\tilde f(t) = f(\max(0, \min(t, 1)))$ is the extension of $f$ to $\mathbb{R}$ by clamping the argument into $[0, 1]$.

results.title: Volterra integrals vanish at the left endpoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $[0, 1]$, the Volterra operator $V$ satisfies $(Vf)(0) = 0$.

results.title: The Volterra operator has norm at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Volterra operator $V$, $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$, acting on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ with the sup norm, has operator norm $\|V\| \le 1$.

results.title: Pointwise factorial bound for powers of the Volterra operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be the Volterra operator $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$. For every natural number $n$, every such function $f$ and every $x \in [0, 1]$, $|(V^n f)(x)| \le \frac{x^n}{n!} \|f\|_\infty$, where $\|f\|_\infty$ is the sup norm of $f$.

results.title: Factorial bound for powers of the Volterra operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be the Volterra operator $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ with the sup norm. For every natural number $n$, the operator norm of $V^n$ satisfies $\|V^n\| \le 1/n!$.

results.title: Nonzero reals lie in the resolvent set of the Volterra operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every nonzero real $z$, $z$ lies in the real resolvent set of the Volterra operator $V$: the bounded operator $z - V$ is invertible.

results.title: The Volterra operator is not invertible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Volterra operator $V$, $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$, on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$ is not a unit in the algebra of bounded linear operators on that space.

results.title: The spectrum of the Volterra operator is `{0}`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The spectrum of the Volterra operator is `{0}`.

results.title: The spectral radius of the Volterra operator is zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be the Volterra operator $(Vf)(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ on the space of bounded continuous real functions on $[0, 1]$. Its spectral radius over the real scalars, the supremum of $|z|$ over real $z$ in the spectrum of $V$, is $0$.

results.title: Index sequences of density one
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A sequence $s \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has density one when it is strictly increasing and $s(n+1)/(n+1) \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$.

results.title: Asymptotically convergent sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real sequence $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is asymptotically convergent to a real number $S$ when there is an index sequence $s$ of density one such that $x_{s(n)} \to S$ as $n \to \infty$.

results.title: Summation by a matrix method
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real matrix $(a_{ik})_{i,k \in \mathbb{N}}$ sums a real sequence $(x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ to a real number $S$ when for every row $i$ the series $\sum_k a_{ik} x_k$ converges unconditionally (equivalently, absolutely) and the row sums $\sum_k a_{ik} x_k$ tend to $S$ as $i \to \infty$.

results.title: Permanent matrix methods
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real matrix $(a_{ik})_{i,k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a permanent (regular, or Toeplitz) method when it sums every convergent real sequence to its limit: for every real sequence $x$ and real number $S$ with $x_n \to S$, the matrix sums $x$ to $S$.

results.title: Bounded sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real sequence $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is bounded when there is a real number $B$ with $|x_n| \le B$ for all $n$.

results.title: The bounded case of Scottish Book Problem 5
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: There is a real matrix $(a_{ik})_{i,k \in \mathbb{N}}$ that is a permanent matrix method such that for every bounded real sequence $x$ and every real number $S$, the matrix sums $x$ to $S$ if and only if $x$ is asymptotically convergent to $S$.

results.title: Negative answer to Scottish Book Problem 5 for bounded sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is no real matrix $(a_{ik})_{i,k \in \mathbb{N}}$ that is a permanent matrix method such that for every bounded real sequence $x$ and every real number $S$, the matrix sums $x$ to $S$ if and only if $x$ is asymptotically convergent to $S$.

results.title: The full 2-shift
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: $X$ is the space of all two-sided sequences $x = (x_i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with every $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$, carrying the product topology.

results.title: The full 3-shift
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The space of all two-sided sequences $y = (y_i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with every $y_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, carrying the product topology. It is the ambient space of the proper 3-colouring shift.

results.title: The proper 3-colouring shift
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: $Y$ is the set of sequences $y = (y_i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ in the full 3-shift (so every $y_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$) such that $y_i \ne y_{i+1}$ for every $i \in \mathbb{Z}$.

results.title: Aperiodic part of the full 2-shift
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be the left shift on the full 2-shift $X$, given by $(\sigma x)_i = x_{i+1}$. The aperiodic part of $X$ is the set of all $x \in X$ that are not periodic for $\sigma$, that is, with $\sigma^n x \ne x$ for every $n \ge 1$.

results.title: Aperiodic part of the 3-colouring shift
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be the left shift on the full 3-shift, given by $(\sigma y)_i = y_{i+1}$. The aperiodic part of the proper 3-colouring shift $Y$ is the set of all $y \in Y$ that are not periodic for $\sigma$, that is, with $\sigma^n y \ne y$ for every $n \ge 1$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be the full 2-shift, $Y$ the proper 3-colouring shift, and $\sigma$ the left shift on each. results.title: Carlitz-type sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For real $q$, a sequence of functions $T_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $n \ge 0$, is Carlitz-type with associated real sequence $(a_k)_{k \ge 0}$ if for every natural number $n$ and every real $x$, $T_n(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} a_k q^{kx}$.

results.title: Carlitz $q$-polynomials $\eta_n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For real $q$, write $[y] = (q^y - 1)/(q - 1)$ and let $a_0 = 1$ and $a_k = k/[k]$ for $k \ge 1$. For natural $n$ and real $x$, Carlitz's $q$-polynomial is $\eta_n(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} a_k q^{kx}$; that is, $(\eta_n)$ is the Carlitz-type sequence with associated sequence $(a_k)$. Its values at $0$ are written $\eta_n = \eta_n(0)$.

results.title: Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli polynomials
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For real $q$, write $[y] = (q^y - 1)/(q - 1)$. For natural $n$ and real $x$, Carlitz's $q$-Bernoulli polynomial is $\beta_n(x) = (q - 1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{n-k} \binom{n}{k} \frac{k + 1}{[k + 1]} q^{kx}$; that is, $(\beta_n)$ is the Carlitz-type sequence with associated sequence $a_k = (k + 1)/[k + 1]$. The Carlitz $q$-Bernoulli numbers are $\beta_n = \beta_n(0)$.

results.caption: Definition

results.title: Edge delta of a path

results.title: Cut capacity

For every set $S$ of vertices with $s \in S$ and $t \notin S$, the net flow leaving $s$ under $f$ is at most the capacity of the cut $S$, namely $\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \notin S} c(u, v)$.

results.title: Residual cut

The residual cut of $c$, $f$ and $s$ is the set of vertices visited by breadth-first search from $s$ in the residual graph of $c$ and $f$, that is, the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in that residual graph.

results.title: Maximality of the Edmonds–Karp flow
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be distinct vertices, and let $f$ be the flow returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$. Then every integer flow $g$ that is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$ has value at $s$ at most the value of $f$ at $s$, where the value of a flow at $s$ is its net flow out of $s$.

results.title: Real capacities
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a capacity function $c$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, the real capacities are the same values viewed as real numbers, $(u, v) \mapsto c(u, v) \in \mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Arc flow of an integer flow
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, its arc flow is the natural-number matrix whose entry at $(u, v)$ is the positive part $\max(f(u, v), 0)$ of $f(u, v)$.

results.title: Real arc flow
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, its real arc flow is the function $(u, v) \mapsto \max(f(u, v), 0)$, the arc flow of $f$, viewed as real numbers.

results.title: A skew flow is the difference of its arc flows
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be an integer flow matrix on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ that is skew-symmetric, $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u, v$, and let $a(u, v) = \max(f(u, v), 0)$ be its arc flow. Then $f(u, v) = a(u, v) - a(v, u)$ for all vertices $u$ and $v$.

results.title: Net outflow in the arc representation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a skew-symmetric integer flow matrix on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, so $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u, v$, and let $a(u, v) = \max(f(u, v), 0)$ be its arc flow, viewed as real numbers. Then for every vertex $v$, $\sum_w a(v, w) - \sum_u a(u, v) = \sum_w f(v, w)$, the net flow leaving $v$.

results.title: A feasible skew flow gives a feasible flow
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values and let $s, t$ be vertices. If an integer flow matrix $f$ is a feasible skew-symmetric $s$-$t$ flow for $c$, then its arc flow $(u, v) \mapsto \max(f(u, v), 0)$, viewed as a real function, is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ viewed as real capacities.

results.title: The Edmonds-Karp residual cut separates source and sink
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. The set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow computed by the Edmonds-Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ is an $s$-$t$ cut: it contains $s$ and not $t$.

results.title: No $s$-$t$ cut is smaller than the Edmonds–Karp residual cut
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Let $S_0$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow computed by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$. results.title: Integral flow theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Then there is a natural-number valued function $f$ on pairs of vertices which, viewed as a real function, is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ whose value is at least the value of every feasible real-valued $s$-$t$ flow for $c$.

results.title: Terminal positions of a placement game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and let $E$ be a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$, the condition under which play has ended. A position $S \subseteq \alpha$ (the set of occupied cells) is terminal when $E(S)$ holds or $S = \alpha$: play has ended, or every cell is occupied. These are the positions with no options.

results.title: Ults of a placement game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and let $E$ be a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$, the condition under which play has ended. A position $S \subseteq \alpha$ is an ult when it is not terminal but has a terminal option: $S$ is not terminal, and there is a cell $c \notin S$ such that $S \cup \{c\}$ is terminal.

results.title: Penults of a placement game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and let $E$ be a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$, the condition under which play has ended. A position $S \subseteq \alpha$ is a penult when it is not terminal and all of its options are ults: $S$ is not terminal, and $S \cup \{c\}$ is an ult for every cell $c \notin S$.

The placement game is the impartial game whose positions are the subsets $S \subseteq \alpha$ (the occupied cells), starting from the empty board $\emptyset$. results.title: Moves of a placement game
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and $E$ a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$ saying when play has ended. In the placement game on $\alpha$ with end predicate $E$, a position $T$ is a move from a position $S$ if and only if $E(S)$ fails and $T = S \cup \{c\}$ for some cell $c \notin S$.

results.title: First-player win in a placement game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and $E$ a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$ saying when play has ended. The player to move from a position $S \subseteq \alpha$ wins the placement game on $\alpha$ with end predicate $E$ when $S$ is not a P-position of that game under normal play, in which the player unable to move loses.

results.title: Normal-play recursion for placement games
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells and $E$ a predicate on subsets of $\alpha$ saying when play has ended. In the placement game on $\alpha$ with end predicate $E$, the player to move from a position $S \subseteq \alpha$ wins if and only if $E(S)$ fails and there is a cell $c \notin S$ such that the player to move from $S \cup \{c\}$ does not win.

results.title: The full board is terminal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set of cells. For every predicate $E$ on subsets of $\alpha$, the full board $\alpha$ is a terminal position of the placement game with ending condition $E$.

results.title: End of Impartial Tic
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write the cells of the $n \times n$ board as pairs $(r, c)$ (row, column) in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}^2$. Impartial Tic has ended at a set $S$ of occupied cells when some row or some column is full: there is a row $r$ with $(r, c) \in S$ for every column $c$, or there is a column $c$ with $(r, c) \in S$ for every row $r$.

results.title: Impartial Tic has not ended on the empty board
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For $n \ge 1$, play of Impartial Tic has not ended on the empty $n \times n$ board: no row and no column is full.

results.title: Orthogonal adjacency
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two cells $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of the $n \times n$ board $\{0, \dots, n-1\}^2$, written as (row, column), are orthogonally adjacent when they lie in the same row and their columns differ by $1$ ($p_1 = q_1$ and $|p_2 - q_2| = 1$), or they lie in the same column and their rows differ by $1$ ($p_2 = q_2$ and $|p_1 - q_1| = 1$).

results.title: The empty board has no Tak road
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$, the empty $n \times n$ board contains no road of Impartial Tak.

results.title: Weights of the Weighted Cross
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $b$, the weight $w(a, b)$ is $0$ if $a, b \in \{0, 4\}$; otherwise it is $2$ if $a = 2$ and $1 \le b \le 3$, or $b = 2$ and $1 \le a \le 3$; and it is $1$ in all other cases. On the $5 \times 5$ window $0 \le a, b \le 4$ this puts weight $0$ at the four corners, $2$ on the central plus (the centre $(2, 2)$ and its four orthogonal neighbours) and $1$ elsewhere.

results.title: Total weight of the Weighted Cross
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The weights $w(a, b)$ of the Weighted Cross over the $5 \times 5$ window sum to $26$: $\sum_{a=0}^{4} \sum_{b=0}^{4} w(a, b) = 26$.

results.title: The first player wins Impartial Tic exactly on odd boards
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, under normal play the first player wins Impartial Tic on the $n \times n$ board, starting from the empty board, if and only if $n$ is odd; for even $n$ the second player wins.

results.title: The second player wins Impartial Tak on even boards
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Impartial Tak is the impartial placement game on the $n \times n$ board in which the players alternately place a token on an empty cell, play ends once the tokens contain a road, and the player unable to move loses. If $n$ is even, the first player does not win from the empty $n \times n$ board, that is, the second player wins.

results.title: The first player wins Impartial Tak on the $5 \times 5$ board
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Impartial Tak is the impartial placement game on the $n \times n$ board in which the players alternately place a token on an empty cell, play ends once the tokens contain a road, and the player unable to move loses. On the $5 \times 5$ board the first player wins from the empty board.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 5$. If $S$ is a penult of Impartial Tic on the $n \times n$ board, then at most $4(n - 2)$ cells of the board lie outside $S$.

results.title: Token counts of dual Impartial Tic penults

results.summary: Let $n \ge 5$ and let $x$ be a natural number with $2n \le x \le 4(n - 2)$. Then there is a penult $S$ of Impartial Tic on the $n \times n$ board such that exactly $x$ cells of the board lie outside $S$.
